svg.title: No fate but what we make
svg.desc: Four-layer defense stack for agentic threats: identity hardening, treating agent text as production code, alerting on edits rather than executions, and responding by revoking triggers before payloads.
svg.text: No fate but what we make
Four boring layers against two compounding curves · each layer names the threat it stops

g.text: IDENTITY — starve the standing access
Short-lived credentials only · no long-lived non-human keys · per-repo OIDC with exact subject matching
· a real inventory of non-human identities · break-glass vaulted
STOPS THE REPLICATION HIGHWAY
no standing access, no persistence
TREAT AGENT TEXT AS PRODUCTION CODE
Instruction files · memory writes · prompt templates · tool and MCP configs — versioned, reviewed,
diffed, change-alerted. The review question: who wrote this sentence, and why does my agent obey it?
STOPS THE TEXT IMPLANT
unreviewed prose is an unguarded gate
DETECT EDITS, NOT EXECUTIONS
Alert on creation and modification of workflows, webhooks, event rules, and memory entries
· declared vs. running drift is an incident, not noise · canary documents and trap instructions
STOPS THE INVISIBILITY
execution looks like work; edits don't
RESPOND IN THE RIGHT ORDER
Revoke triggers before removing payloads — cleanup is itself a tripwire · treat config and secret reads
during the window as tainted · purge time (scheduled jobs, queued sends) · roll back memory, not just creds
STOPS THE RESURRECTION
your remediation job is their heartbeat
None of this is exotic — boring, on purpose. Boring is the match for a threat arriving as two boring curves.
1984's version needed a time machine and a factory. 2026's needs a stolen key, a retry loop, and one org that never reviewed the files its agents read.
